channel.title: Disequilibrium
channel.description: A weekly newsletter on how AI is changing the entry-level job market.

item.title: AI is repricing the entry-level job rather than deleting it — September 29, 2026
item.description: The best national data found no AI-driven unemployment spike among recent graduates, while economists made their sharpest cut yet to college-graduate wage expectations. You still get hired, but the degree no longer sets what you are worth.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

What does a college degree still buy you? Two teams answered this week, and the answers split. AI is repricing the entry-level job rather than deleting it. You still get hired, but the degree no longer sets what you are worth. A National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) paper found no rise in unemployment among recent graduates this summer, relative to older graduates or young workers without degrees. Four days earlier, 123 economists surveyed by Indeed Hiring Lab made their largest single cut yet to what they expect college-educated workers to earn, while holding flat for workers without degrees. Getting hired and getting paid are separate questions, and only the second one is moving. Underemployment, which counts graduates working jobs that do not need their degree, sits at 42%. Employers are also building new doors. KPMG kept its graduate intake, and law firms are paying up to $438,000 for technical roles. The rest of this issue is about where the price of an entry-level job is being reset, and how to compare offers on what they teach and pay over time rather than on the credential that got you in.

Tech

Recent graduates are not losing jobs to AI at a measurable rate, but economists cut their outlook for college-graduate real wages from 47.3 to 42.4. Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu analyzed Current Population Survey data from June through August and found no increase in relative unemployment for recent college graduates. In Indeed Hiring Lab's survey, where 50 is neutral, the same reading for workers without degrees held at 50.9. For CS majors weighing offers, the credential no longer sets a wage floor, so compare offers on where the pay and the work lead, not the starting number. (NBER | Indeed Hiring Lab)

Performance marketing agencies say they have stopped hiring college graduates at all. At a Digiday town hall on September 24, one agency owner said, "We haven't hired college-level grads in some time, and I don't anticipate that we will be." The tasks that once justified a graduate salary, such as building keyword lists, pulling reports and checking placements, no longer carry one. A Stanford-based finding puts the employment loss for workers aged 18 to 34 in AI-exposed occupations at 16%. Here the rung is removed rather than repriced. For marketing and communications majors, an agency with a named graduate training program is a real differentiator (PPC Land)

Finance & Consulting

The Big Four accounting firms are keeping their graduate intake and changing what graduates do in it. At KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC, AI now handles the data entry and report production that used to fill a trainee's first two years. KPMG front-loads technical and regulatory exams so graduates finish them before client work, and chief people officer Marc Burrows said that graduates will be "more involved in reviewing and exercising judgement rather than simply producing outputs." For accounting and finance students, ask a Big Four recruiter which tasks a first-year owns and when the first judgment call happens, because the firms have publicly committed to moving it earlier. (City A.M.)

McKinsey, BCG and Bain are all testing AI skills inside the case interview itself. The three firms are experimenting with letting candidates use AI during cases and with other ways to assess AI capability as part of the screen. MIT Sloan's career office reports that the change has created real anxiety among candidates who prepared for the traditional format. No firm has published a standard format yet. If you are recruiting for consulting this cycle, practice casing with a model in the room and be ready to explain why you accepted or rejected what it told you. (MIT Sloan Career Development Office)

Seventy percent of 376 provosts use AI at least weekly, but only 20% say their institution has a coherent vision for AI in teaching. Inside Higher Ed and Hanover Research surveyed provosts at public and private nonprofit institutions in July and August. Only 10% report a centralized AI strategy. For students recruiting into finance and consulting, the AI fluency these firms now test is something you will likely have to build outside your degree requirements. Of AI skill mentions on resumes, 74% are tied to real projects rather than coursework. (Inside Higher Ed | CNBC)

Law

Law firms are building in-house AI teams that pay up to $438,000, a second career ladder beside the associate track. Cooley launched Cooley AI, a firm-owned AI company with 14 open positions, and advertises $220,000 to $250,000 for a senior AI data engineer. One unnamed firm posted up to $438,000 for a director of applied AI. Kirkland & Ellis committed $500 million to a custom AI platform over three to four years, and Morgan & Morgan at least $1 billion over a decade. For law students with any technical background, price this door against the associate track everyone else is lining up for. (JD Journal)

AI companies are recruiting lawyers out of large firms into a new role called legal engineer. The role pairs legal training with specifying, testing and supervising legal AI systems, and vendors including Harvey advertise it openly. The pull is on qualified lawyers rather than new graduates, so it draws experience out of the firms while they cut the intake that would replace it. For 1Ls, track the posted requirements for legal engineer roles now to see how much practice experience vendors demand before they will hire you. (Law.com)

item.title: The AI job market is growing but hiring almost only seniors — September 22, 2026
item.description: Two independent datasets found employment and pay rising at AI-adopting firms while the junior share of postings collapsed. The entry-level problem is a missing bottom rung rather than weak demand.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

At companies that adopted AI last year, total headcount went up. A working paper covering 41 countries, 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records found employment at those firms grew 3.3%, with senior roles up 6.7% and junior roles down about 3%. The AI job market is growing and hiring, but almost all of that growth sits in senior roles, so the entry-level problem is a missing bottom rung rather than weak demand. That distinction changes what you do about it. Weak demand means waiting for the cycle to turn. A missing rung means the job you want may never be posted at the level you are applying to. The damage shows up as a slower search rather than no job. A new National Bureau of Economic Research paper finds job-finding and job-switching rates falling for AI-exposed workers, and the natural rate of unemployment up roughly 0.1 to 0.2 points since large language models arrived. The rest of this issue is about which employers are hiring upward, the one industry where the ladder held, and the two states that will now tell you why an algorithm rejected you.

Tech

Two research teams measured the same market from opposite ends this week and both found the junior share of hiring collapsing while total employment rose. Bharat Chandar of Stanford and Bouke Klein Teeselink of King's College London found senior employment at AI-adopting firms up 6.7% while junior employment fell about 3%. Indeed Hiring Lab found advertised pay in the most AI-exposed occupations up about 46% since 2021, but that premium disappears once you control for seniority, because entry-level postings in those fields fell from 29% of the total to 10% while senior postings rose from 22% to 47%. If an AI wage premium looks like a reason to enter a field, check the seniority mix of its openings first. (Bloomberg | Insurance Journal | Indeed Hiring Lab)

Oracle told investors in writing that AI adoption has resulted in reductions to its workforce, after cutting about 21,000 jobs in fiscal 2026. The disclosure sits in the company's annual report, and another round began on September 14. PayPal cut 251 headquarters jobs and said it expects a further 20% reduction over the next few years in order to invest more in AI. KPMG trimmed about 4% of its Advisory division, and the cuts landed on its AI, cyber, SAP and testing teams. For students targeting consulting, an AI practice group is not automatically the safe place to land, so ask whether that team sells billable client delivery or internal capability. (Martin Cid Magazine | Crunchbase News | The Register)

Ethan Mollick argues the models already have far more capability than anyone is using, and names four things they still lack. Deep domain expertise, wide interdisciplinary knowledge, taste and agency. He cites Anthropic research indicating that expertise shapes the quality of what a model returns, so experts get better output from the same system. As generation gets cheap, curation becomes the scarce skill. For students deciding how to spend the next two years, going deep enough in one subject to know when a model is wrong about it beats collecting another tool on your resume. (One Useful Thing)

Law

Demand for large-firm attorney hours grew 4.2% in the first half of 2026 against a historic norm near 1.5%, with revenue up 11.7%. Thomson Reuters and Bloomberg Law data show AI behaving as a complement to billable hours rather than a substitute, because cheaper legal work per unit is inducing clients to buy more of it. Law is the counterexample to this week's other numbers. For pre-law students, the question to put to a firm is whether that growth is being staffed with junior associates or with contract and lateral hires. (TaxProf Blog | Thomson Reuters Institute)

Latitude Legal, which grew new clients 52% in the first half of 2026, staffs almost entirely former law firm partners and senior in-house counsel. The flexible-talent provider named Alex Su president this week, and his argument is that as AI improves, demand rises for lawyers with the judgment to direct it and own the result. The fastest-growing part of the legal market never touches the junior rung. For law students, that makes a first job whose purpose is supervised reps of real client work the thing worth optimizing for. (LawNext)

Among 486 summer associates surveyed this year, 96% used AI during their program, up from 80% a year earlier, and 9% of firms now required it. Law360 Pulse found 97% using it for legal research and only 1% of firms discouraging it. Meanwhile at least 12 law schools rewrote their AI policies over the summer, and about a quarter now ban it outright. For rising 2Ls, AI use is the floor in a summer program, so what distinguishes you is being able to say why you rejected an AI answer. (Law360 Pulse)

Government & Policy

California's legislature passed four workplace AI bills that become law automatically if the governor does not act by September 30, and none of them covers hiring. SB 947 requires human review and written notice when discipline or termination relies primarily on an automated system. SB 951 expands the state's layoff-notice law so mass-layoff notices must name the job functions being automated. AB 1883 bans emotion recognition and neural-data collection on employees. Candidate screening, the front door of the pipeline, is untouched. For applicants, assume no right to an explanation when an algorithm screens you out in California. (National Law Review)

States filed 155 bills on AI in the workplace this year and enacted two. MultiState's session review found Colorado's SB 189 and Connecticut's SB 5 are the only ones that became law, and both require employers using automated hiring tools to notify applicants, explain an adverse outcome in detail, allow a request for human review, and correct inaccurate personal data. Applicant-notification bills died in Minnesota, Iowa and New York. If you are applying to employers in Colorado or Connecticut, ask in writing for that explanation and that review after a screening-stage rejection, because almost nowhere else can you. (MultiState)

item.title: AI is taking the beginner tasks that used to train new hires — September 15, 2026
item.description: A randomized trial at eleven law firms found junior lawyers kept none of their AI-assisted gains once the tool was removed. Employers say the blocker to early-career hiring is inexperience, not AI.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

In a study released this week, 133 patent lawyers at eleven firms spent 90 days drafting with an AI tool, and then the researchers took it away and scored their work blind. AI is absorbing the beginner tasks that used to turn a new hire into a competent one, so the thing to judge a first job on now is whether it still teaches you anything. The juniors had gained the most while the tool was running, and kept none of it on average once it was gone. The low-stakes work that used to build judgment is now done by something that does not need to learn. Employers are not pulling back from early-career hiring, though. ManpowerGroup surveyed 39,878 employers this week and found 45% adding more early-career talent than last year against 20% pulling back, and they blamed candidate inexperience more often than AI for the roles they cut. The demand is there. The apprenticeship inside it is coming apart, and the rest of this issue is about where that is happening and what to ask an employer to tell the difference.

Law

Large law firms are on track to hire roughly 2,000 fewer new lawyers this year than in 2024, and two-thirds expect smaller first-year classes in 2028 than in 2025. Bloomberg Law reported the Citi figures, which also put second-year summer classes at their lowest since 2020. No recession is driving this contraction. Firm leaders say they cannot forecast how much junior work AI will absorb. For 1Ls, the 2L summer slot is the bottleneck now, so treat recruiting timelines as fixed and widen your list past the largest firms. (Bloomberg Law | Above the Law)

In that patent-drafting trial, the junior lawyers who gained most from the AI kept none of it once the tool was gone. David Autor and co-authors ran the 90-day experiment with 133 attorneys, with blinded evaluators scoring enforceability, accuracy, completeness and clarity. Junior scores bifurcated rather than rising, producing fewer mediocre drafts but more poor ones and more good ones. Senior attorneys kept their gains. It is the first causal evidence that AI-assisted junior work builds expertise or hollows it out depending on how the workflow is arranged. That turns a vague worry into one callback question. Does a junior here write a first draft before touching the tool? (Patently-O | NBER)

Across 109 UK firms, training contract places fell by 44 seats, with Linklaters cutting its intake from 100 to 60 and Freshfields from 85 to 70. Legal Cheek attributes the largest cuts primarily to firms expanding solicitor apprenticeships rather than to AI. The training is being moved to a different entrance rather than eliminated. For students targeting UK law, check which of your firms are growing apprenticeship intakes, because that may now be the higher-probability door into the same building. (Legal Cheek)

Tech

Anthropic says Claude now writes about 80% of its code and that each of its engineers ships roughly eight times what one shipped from 2021 to 2025. The company stated that writing code is no longer the constraint. IEEE Spectrum reported the same shift elsewhere, with AI writing 42% of code added to shared codebases while 96% of developers say they do not fully trust it, and found firms rebuilding junior onboarding around review. IBM now gives juniors harder projects sooner and has them troubleshoot the failures. For computer science majors, a story about a plausible-looking AI bug you caught is worth more than another finished project. (Anthropic | IEEE Spectrum)

Entry-level postings in computer and mathematical occupations in New York City are down 49% since 2022, a steeper fall than in any other field. The Center for an Urban Future found roles with the highest AI exposure lost 29% of their entry-level postings while roles with minimal exposure gained 21%, and postings requiring AI skills grew 20%. For computer science and data students, the dataset that measures the collapse also shows where the demand went, so one documented AI project beats another round of applications. (The City Reporter | Center for an Urban Future)

Meta is asking engineers whether they want to become managers again, a year after cutting about 8,000 jobs and scrapping 6,000 open roles to flatten the company. Fortune reported that the Applied AI division is putting the question to individual contributors, even as headcount fell 3% quarter over quarter to 75,472. The coordination layer AI was supposed to remove has come back. If you are targeting large tech employers, the reopening roles reward organizing other people's work around an AI system. (Fortune)

Healthcare

California's legislature passed two bills barring AI from replacing a licensed professional's clinical judgment, and the governor has until September 30 to act. AB 2575 also protects health workers who override an AI output from retaliation. The same week, Dhruv Khullar argued in a New England Journal of Medicine perspective that AI is more likely to grow the clinical workforce than shrink it, because cheaper cataract surgery and joint replacement raised volumes and employment. Healthcare's training ladder has a legal floor under it that law's and engineering's do not. For pre-meds and nursing students, finishing licensure remains the highest-leverage move available. (National Nurses United | NEJM)

Ambient AI scribes let emergency physicians at Brigham and Women's Hospital document faster without moving a single patient through the department any quicker. Christopher Baugh, an emergency physician there, described 152 patients waiting against 61 acute care rooms and said the scribes have not changed the status quo. Oracle Health shipped a nurse-facing AI agent the same week into a workforce where only 41% of nurses use AI regularly against 57% of physicians. Scribing is one of the few paid apprenticeships in medicine, and the typing is the part being automated. If you use scribe work for clinical hours, pitch yourself on chart review rather than on speed. (STAT News | Healthcare Dive)

item.title: AI is moving out of the layoff statistics and into the fine print — September 8, 2026
item.description: UBS now scores 2027 graduate applicants on how they actually use AI, 25,000 Kaiser nurses picketed for contract limits on it, and California sent 16 AI bills to the governor. A written rule tells you what will be asked of you in advance.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

If you apply to UBS for a 2027 graduate seat, the interview will ask how you actually use AI. Name a real task, what you handed a model, and what came back better. UBS is among the first large banks to write that requirement down. AI is moving out of the layoff statistics and into the fine print, meaning the interview rubric, the union contract and the state law.

A layoff number tells you what already happened to someone else. A written rule tells you what will be asked of you, in advance. The statistics this week moved the other way. Challenger, Gray & Christmas, an outplacement firm, found AI cited in only 3,462 August job cuts, its lowest monthly total since December 2025. The Economist reported that the gap between unemployment among 20-to-24-year-olds and the overall rate sits near a multi-decade low.

The rest of this issue is about where the fine print got written this week, in hiring criteria, a nurses’ contract and a fee agreement. You can read it before you sign anything.

Finance & Consulting

UBS made demonstrated AI ability an entry criterion for its 2027 graduate and intern class in Global Banking and Markets. Interviews now ask how candidates use the tools, and those hired enter an internal AI Fluency Pathway. OpenAI began rolling out GPT-6 Astra the same week, able to generate documents, spreadsheets and decks on a firm’s own templates. That is the first-year analyst deliverable. For finance recruits, start logging tasks where you can explain what you fed a model and how you checked it. (Financial Times | CNBC)

Santander and Coursera released 50,000 more free places on AI and data courses, bringing the program to 100,000, with no degree required. Demand moved the same week on campus, where a Michigan State course in computational and AI literacy is now full after failing to launch twice in 2025 for lack of enrollment. For students who need evidence for the interview UBS now runs, this is the cheapest way to get it. (Banco Santander | The State News)

Balyasny launched an AI Fellowship Program in New York paying up to $225,000 that rotates hires onto trading desks. Fellows start with the central AI team, then run three-month rotations as the dedicated AI partner to a portfolio manager. For technical students, this is a front-office path that skips the shrinking analyst class. (eFinancialCareers)

Healthcare

More than 25,000 Kaiser Permanente nurses picketed 22 California hospitals on September 1, demanding contract limits on AI. They want a formal role in deciding how AI tools reach patient care. Days earlier, the state legislature passed 16 AI bills, now on Governor Newsom’s desk. One of them, sponsored by the same union, would bar AI from independently performing any clinical function that requires a licensed professional. If you are entering a licensed field, read the AI language in the contract before you sign. (National Nurses United | Bloomberg Law)

Twelve utilization-review nurses at Montefiore Medical Center were terminated in July, their work absorbed by software from Datavant. The New York State Nurses Association calls it one of the first documented cases of US health professionals displaced by AI, and has filed a grievance. Those nurses had won a contract containing automation protections months earlier, after a 41-day strike. For nursing students, the exposed work here is chart review and insurer negotiation, not bedside care. (NJTODAY.NET)

Becker’s Hospital Review ranked transcriptionists, coders and patient-access representatives as the health roles most exposed to AI, and projected health information technologists and registrars to grow 16% by 2035. The same week, OpenAI connected ChatGPT Health to Epic, the records system covering more than 325 million patients, for pre-visit review and handoff summaries. For health informatics majors, the growth is on the side of the degree that builds and audits systems, not the side that processes records. (Becker's Hospital Review | TechCrunch)

Law

Legora ran OpenAI’s new Astra model on financial statement tie-out and its agent checked 41 documents in one run in minutes, catching all four errors Legora had planted, including a £500,000 gap hidden in a revenue note. Harvey said that Astra approaches legal work the way a discerning lawyer does. Multi-document cross-checking in diligence is a junior’s classic first real assignment. For law students, build the pitch around reviewing and defending agent output rather than producing the first draft. (Artificial Lawyer)

Above the Law argued that firms get no return on client-facing legal AI, because it cuts billable hours and billable hours are the revenue. By that logic the only clean win is back-office automation, which is why firms champion AI publicly and move slowly on billable work. Kyra Law, a UK firm built around AI from the start, launched the same week publishing fixed fees far below traditional rates. For 1Ls, a firm’s fee structure predicts its AI adoption better than its press releases. (Above the Law | Artificial Lawyer)

A LexisNexis survey found that 15% of lawyers at large UK firms now describe themselves as dependent on AI to do their job. The top three uses are drafting, legal research and document review, which is the first-year associate’s day. Vendors are also shifting the pitch from a generic junior associate to a doppelganger calibrated on one lawyer’s writing. For summer associates, get a real partner to mark up your work, because the tool cannot manufacture that. (Artificial Lawyer | Above the Law)

item.title: Finished work no longer proves you can do it — September 1, 2026
item.description: A Wall Street bank, six health system CEOs and an MIT committee named the same problem in one week. Evaluation is moving to live, unassisted demonstration.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

Bill Gates published a 6,000-word essay Wednesday arguing that the jobs at most risk are entry- and mid-level, and that the work replacing them requires “skills that take many years to learn.” He did not name the mechanism. Three other institutions did. Finished work no longer proves you can do it, so the test is moving to whether you can explain it live.

Goldman Sachs gave the clearest version. Junior traders learned judgment by pricing client requests under supervision, work the firm can now automate. That removes the task that trained the junior and the one that proved the junior was any good. Employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations runs 19% below its less-exposed peers’ trend, according to Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab, driven by reduced hiring.

The aggregate market is steadier than that sounds. On August 28, the Bureau of Labor Statistics preliminarily revised payroll growth down by 79,000 through March, a 0.1% markdown against a 0.2% decade average. What is changing is which jobs exist, not how many. The rest of this issue is about which finished products stopped counting as proof.

Finance & Consulting

Chris Churchman, the Goldman Sachs partner running its AI build, warned that automating junior work risks “cognitive atrophy” among bankers. He asked whether automating the apprenticeship still produces senior traders who understand their work. OpenAI published matching evidence two days later. Among more than 1,000 Bocconi University undergraduates, those given ChatGPT scored almost a full point higher on a five-point rubric, but only critical-thinking training produced a wider range of ideas. For finance majors, ask what an analyst class still does by hand, because that shrinking list is the training. (TheStreet | OpenAI)

Bayer is running 30 AI agents on its systems overhaul with the stated goal of needing “significantly fewer consultants.” Jochen Kamp, who leads it, said “fewer and fewer” traditional consultants will be needed. Source Global, a research firm, found 55% of clients plan to use the Big Four accounting firms more over the next 12 months, down from 80% a year earlier. The exposed work is implementation, where analysts sit. If you are recruiting at a Big Four firm or Accenture, ask what share of the practice’s revenue comes from advice. (The Irish Times)

An MIT committee reported that employers already weight interview problem-solving over grades, the same week a study found that AI cannot grade written work reliably. The report notes employers care less about grades than about “performance on internal assessments, such as the ability to answer difficult interview questions.” Researchers who ran 50 bioscience essays through ChatGPT found gaps against human markers as large as 40 points on a 100-point scale, inflating weak essays and marking down strong ones. For anyone recruiting this fall, practice explaining your reasoning out loud on AI-assisted work. (Inside Higher Ed | Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education)

Law

Google Cloud launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal on August 25 with Weil, Cleary and Freshfields among its first firms. It executes complete workflows rather than assisting with tasks, and the four it names are contract review, due diligence, regulatory monitoring and privacy requests. That list is the standard first-year associate rotation. Weil’s co-managing partner said clients now expect firms to use AI and pass on the efficiencies. For 1Ls heading into interviews, ask what junior work looks like once these agents run. (Google Cloud | Artificial Lawyer)

The chief executive of Harvey, a legal AI company, said the question is no longer the product roadmap but “what it will do to the profession.” Winston Weinberg spoke at ILTACON, where a veteran executive quoted by the legal journalist Bob Ambrogi said the industry has hit “peak legal tech.” Practitioners want something narrower. In a survey of 400 US legal professionals by the software company 8am, 42% most want AI aimed at time tracking, and 39% lose four or more billable hours a week to admin. For law students, legal-operations fluency is an opening almost nobody claims. (Artificial Lawyer | ABA Journal)

Healthcare

Executives at six health systems named AI adoption without reskilling the most dangerous trend in healthcare. Leaders from Baystate Health, Cincinnati Children’s, Banner Health and Duke Health told Becker’s Hospital Review adoption is outrunning investment in people. Cincinnati Children’s chief executive Steve Davis warned that moving staff into AI-enabled workflows without “deliberate development of the critical thinking and analytical skills” risks weakening what the tools are meant to augment. That is the Goldman warning in another industry. For pre-health students, take a first clinical job only if it still makes you do the reasoning. (Becker's Hospital Review)

On August 27, National Nurses United held its largest coordinated action against Palantir, with protests in eight cities. The 225,000-member union objects to HCA Healthcare’s Timpani platform, built on Palantir technology, which nurses say moves staffing decisions to a Nashville office and displaces nurse managers’ judgment about unit staffing. HCA says nurse leaders review and edit the generated schedules. The complaint is not that jobs disappear but that judgment relocates. For nursing students, ask who sets the unit schedule and staffing ratio. (Healthcare IT News | National Nurses United)

Northwell Health is building a clinical informatics rotation into residency as its northern region finishes an ambient AI rollout that took 18 months. Albert Villarin, its chief medical informatics officer, said the rollout reaches nurses by year-end, against roughly 18 years for the shift from paper to electronic records. He argues AI has to be taught like a stethoscope rather than “discovered in practice.” Northwell is the only institution here replacing the training it automates. For pre-meds, ask whether target residency programs run an informatics rotation. (Becker's Hospital Review)

item.title: The jobs coming back are the ones that check AI's work — August 25, 2026
item.description: Three economists spent the week disagreeing about whether AI is causing anything at all. Employers are settling it in practice.
item.content:encoded:
What Changed This Week

Three prominent economists spent this week disagreeing in public about whether AI is causing anything at all. The entry-level jobs coming back are the ones that check AI's work.

Stanford's Erik Brynjolfsson argues that large language models absorb codified knowledge, the written-down kind new graduates start out selling. Harvard's David Deming counters that junior hiring began falling roughly six months before ChatGPT shipped and blames remote work. While they argue, employers are settling it in practice. Toptal, a talent marketplace, found demand for experienced finance consultants up 31% in a single quarter, and Robert Half found that 32% of managers who cut roles after deploying AI later hired for the same or similar ones. Firms that assumed the technology could do the analysis alone are now paying people to check it.

The rest of this issue covers where checking that output is becoming a job, what a federal regulator proposed to make the standard, and why the skill employers want is not the one being handed out for free. You do not control how many entry-level jobs exist. You do control whether you are the person who can tell if the answer is correct.

Finance & Consulting

Demand for experienced finance consultants rose 31% in one quarter, and 32% of managers who cut roles after deploying AI later rehired for the same or similar ones. Toptal's second-quarter report ranks finance the strongest of the ten segments it tracks, up 39% year over year. Chief economist Erik Stettler attributes the jump to a correction. Firms assumed AI could handle financial analysis on its own, and are now hiring people to evaluate deployments, assess risk, and validate what the models produce. Robert Half found finance had the highest rehire rate of any sector, at 44%. For finance and economics majors, the refilled roles are judgment applied to model output, which is a job function you can train for. (Toptal via Stacker)

The optimists and the skeptics are quoting the same dataset. Sander van 't Noordende, chief executive of the recruiting firm Randstad, argued in Forbes that consensus is shifting from displacement toward expansion, citing a Ramp and Revelio study finding that the organizations investing most heavily in AI grew headcount by over 10% and entry-level hiring by 12%. Anders Humlum, the University of Chicago economist, cited that same study to NPR to make the same point. Randstad's own data shows demand for emotional intelligence up 173% and for creativity up 168%. If you are choosing between two similar employers this fall, the one visibly spending on AI is the one more likely to be growing its junior ranks. (Forbes | NPR)

Roughly 76% of Santander UK's graduate intake entered AI and data programs this year, up from 45%. Bloomberg reported that AI now shapes bank internships as much as the hours do, with interns building agents and running demonstrations for senior bankers. That reverses the direction of the apprenticeship. Juniors used to absorb judgment from above by grinding through analyst work, and are now valued for showing senior staff what the tool does. For students recruiting into banking, the demo is doing work the pitch book used to do. (Bloomberg)

Healthcare

The Food and Drug Administration proposed evaluating generative AI medical devices the way it evaluates physicians. The agency's August 18 discussion paper describes a competency assessment explicitly modeled on how doctors are trained, running from non-clinical benchmarking through clinical confirmation under real-world conditions to ongoing postmarket monitoring. Devices would be scored on two axes, how independently a function acts and how severe the consequence of a wrong output. A federal regulator has written the supervised-judgment pipeline medical students train inside into a proposed standard for machines. For pre-med and health-policy students, comments are open under docket FDA-2026-N-7874 until October 19, and a comment on the public record is something you can file this semester. (FDA | Healio)

Tech

Apple cut roughly 200 roles across Siri, Vision Pro, and its AI integration teams without reducing its bet on AI. About 100 positions went from the Vision Pro organization and about 100 from Siri and related software teams. Reporting indicates that the Siri cuts targeted staff who worked on the older architecture, because the new large-language-model Siri shipping with iOS 27 requires different expertise. Apple rarely announces layoffs, which makes the composition of these cuts unusually legible. For computer science majors, this suggests the risk is not that your job disappears but that the stack you specialized in stops being the one your employer needs. (Bloomberg | TechCrunch)

Anthropic launched a free AI course platform the same week employers rated AI skills the weakest thing graduates bring. Claude Academy opened on August 20 with courses accessible without an account, and completion badges for signed-in users that post to LinkedIn, built around a framework of delegating work to a model and then verifying it. Inside Higher Ed reported data from the National Association of Colleges and Employers showing that as of March, 35% of entry-level jobs required AI skills, up from 13% six months earlier. Those same employers rank AI skills below teamwork, communication, critical thinking, and leadership among what graduates arrive with. The badge is cheap signal worth having in an afternoon. The gap employers describe is knowing when not to use the tool, and no free course currently certifies that. (Anthropic | Inside Higher Ed)
